content: 1. Pompeii JA and Molina Flores B, along with their colleagues, discussed the challenges faced in the final stages of implementing a regional rabies elimination program. Their findings were published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science in 2017. 2. Vigilato MAN, Cosivi O, Knöbl T, Clavijo A, and Silva HMT provided an update on rabies control efforts in Latin America and the Caribbean, emphasizing the progress and challenges in the region. This was detailed in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2013. 3. The Rabies Elimination Program in Bangladesh, as highlighted by the World Health Organization (WHO), showcases a national effort to eradicate rabies through mass dog vaccination and public awareness campaigns. 4. Lapiz SMD, Miranda MEG, Garcia RG, Daguro LI, Paman MD, Madrinan FP, and their team implemented an intersectoral program in the Philippines, known as the Bohol Rabies Prevention and Elimination Project. This initiative successfully targeted both human and canine rabies, as reported in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2012. 5. A comprehensive rationale for investing in the elimination of dog-mediated human rabies was outlined, emphasizing the cost-effectiveness and public health benefits of such efforts. 6. Harischandra PL, Gunesekera A, Janakan N, Gongal G, and Abela-Ridder B documented Sri Lanka's progress toward achieving zero rabies deaths by 2020. Their findings were published in the WHO South-East Asia Journal of Public Health in 2016. 7. Mpolya EA, Lembo T, Lushasi K, Mancy R, Mbunda EM, Makungu S, and colleagues shared their experiences from a large-scale rabies elimination demonstration project in southern Tanzania. Their work, published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science in 2017, highlighted the importance of tailored strategies for different countries, robust data systems, and operational research to maximize cost-effectiveness in the final stages of rabies elimination. 8. The United Against Rabies collaboration regularly monitors and reports on the progress of rabies elimination programs globally. This includes annual reviews of activities, budgets, and outcomes to ensure transparency and accountability. 9. Access to rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins is a critical component of the global strategic plan for rabies elimination. Vaccine banks, modeled after successful stockpiles for diseases like cholera and yellow fever, aim to ensure timely and affordable access to life-saving biologics. 10. Vaccine banks operate as centralized procurement and distribution systems, reducing costs, ensuring a stable supply of quality-assured vaccines, and incentivizing manufacturers to increase production. These banks have been instrumental in addressing neglected diseases and catalyzing effective control programs. 11. Integrated Bite Case Management (IBCM) is a strategy to assess the risk of rabies exposure following dog bites. By determining whether post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is necessary, IBCM reduces unnecessary use of rabies biologics while maintaining effective treatment for high-risk cases. 12. IBCM requires collaboration between human and animal health sectors to evaluate the risk of rabies in biting animals and provide appropriate treatment to bite victims. This approach improves case detection, reduces treatment costs, and enhances surveillance quality. 13. The Stepwise Approach to Rabies Elimination (SARE) is a tool designed to help countries develop national plans, enhance intersectoral collaboration, and measure progress toward rabies elimination. It emphasizes key activities such as dog vaccination, public awareness, PEP accessibility, and diagnostic capacity. 14. Ethiopia, with one of the highest rabies death rates in Africa, utilized the SARE tool in 2016 to assess its rabies control capacity. This self-assessment identified critical gaps, such as limited access to dog vaccines and poor intersectoral collaboration, while highlighting strengths like existing surveillance systems and outbreak response legislation. 15. The establishment of vaccine banks for rabies, modeled after successful initiatives like the oral cholera vaccine stockpile, has demonstrated the potential to shift focus from disease response to active prevention and control. These banks ensure sustainable access to vaccines and catalyze national and regional rabies elimination efforts.
